title: Please define “to teach”
author: John Wills Lloyd
summary: Special educator John Wills Lloyd sets out to find an objective, operational definition of teaching that can anchor later discussion of research and practice. He moves through popular uses of the word, well-known inspirational quotations, expert definitions, and lists of evidence-based practices such as Rosenshine’s principles and the high-leverage practices, finding the first two too vague and the last too molecular to serve as a definition. His proposal is Barbara Bateman’s 1971 formulation that teaching is the manipulation of environmental variables to cause predicted changes in behavior. He then defends each term in turn, arguing that teachers necessarily manipulate their environment, that learning can only be ascertained through behavior, that teaching must cause outcomes, and that the teacher must predict in advance what will change. He closes by urging educators, and special educators in particular, to judge the flood of teaching recommendations against this no-nonsense standard.
points: Lloyd rejects inspirational quotations about teaching because none describe what a teacher actually does in observable terms.
Rosenshine’s principles and the high-leverage practices move toward countable actions but are too molecular to define teaching itself.
He adopts Bateman’s definition that teaching is the manipulation of environmental variables to cause predicted changes in behavior.
The word "cause" rules out the excuse "I taught it, they just didn’t get it," since teaching is judged by whether learning follows.
Requiring a prediction stops teachers from claiming credit for whatever students happen to do later, echoing Mager’s insistence on stated objectives.
quotes: I decided we ought to take a look at the meaning of “teaching,” so I wrote this post. I wanted to work toward an objective definition of teaching that could provide structure to future posts about research, effectiveness, and practice.

Though such popular uses may communicate an idea about teaching in the context in which they are used, these everyday uses are rarely based on a careful analysis of the meaning of the word “teach.” They are usually a kind of short hand for an idea about something sort of vague.
None of these quotations, however, provide objective and operational descriptions of teaching. They do not tell what the teacher does in observable terms.

The Rosenshine principles, the HLPs, and other descriptions of particular parts of teaching are helpful because they move us more toward talking about actions that can be coded, counted, But they are a bit too molecular to serve as a definition of teaching.
Some folks might say that learning isn’t really about behavior, but they will ultimately have to admit that the only way to ascertain whether someone has learned something is to assess behavior.
Well, what about the word “cause?” That word is exactly the right one. Teaching must produce outcomes. There should be a direct and dang near linear connection between teaching and learning.
One should not hope to get credit simply for throwing the dart; one wants the dart to hit the target—and preferably the center ring on the target.
I see too many recommendations about teaching that address unobservable processes and subjective outcomes.
